article.headline: The 800-Volt Semiconductor Index and Wolfspeed's Second Act
article.lede: An image circulating on X shows the constituent list of MSXX800V, a Morgan Stanley proprietary index backing thirteen semiconductor and power-hardware companies on the 800-volt transition — the voltage standard now reshaping both electric-vehicle drivetrains and AI data centres. The dry caption — “just gonna leave this here as $WOLF makes the rounds” — points to the basket’s most provocative member: Wolfspeed, which emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy eight months ago and sits at 5.18% weight alongside Navitas Semiconductor. Whether the comment reads as validation or quiet scepticism, the index is a considered claim worth unpacking.
article.body:
The image shows the constituent list of **MSXX800V**, a proprietary index administered by Morgan Stanley (MS)’s *Trading and Investment Solutions* (TIS) group — almost certainly the reference underlier for one or more structured notes sold to institutional and private-wealth clients. Proprietary MSXX-prefixed indices are not publicly documented; their rules and composition appear only inside SEC Form 424B2 prospectus supplements. The thirteen names span the full *silicon carbide* (SiC) and *gallium nitride* (GaN) power-semiconductor supply chain, from substrate makers through chip designers to the power-distribution hardware that routes 800 volts into data-centre racks. The poster’s dry caption — “just gonna leave this here as $WOLF makes the rounds” — draws attention to Wolfspeed (WOLF), which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in June 2025 and emerged ninety-one days later; it sits at 5.18% weight, joint-sixth in the basket alongside Navitas Semiconductor (NVTS).

An 800-volt architecture doubles the system supply voltage relative to the 400V standard that has dominated both EV drivetrains and data-centre power distribution. Halving the current for the same power level cuts resistive heat losses by roughly 75%, enabling sub-20-minute 80% charge times in the first commercial 800V electric vehicles. The theme’s more recent, and possibly larger, driver is artificial intelligence infrastructure: NVIDIA (NVDA) announced at Computex 2025 that its next-generation *Kyber* rack systems for Rubin Ultra GPUs would standardise on 800-volt *HVDC* (high-voltage direct current) power distribution across the data-centre floor. At gigawatt scale, 800V versus legacy 54V rack-level distribution cuts copper cabling by 45%, eliminates several AC-to-DC conversion stages, and recovers up to five percentage points of end-to-end efficiency. Nine of the thirteen basket constituents were subsequently named official NVIDIA 800V silicon-provider ecosystem partners.

Constituent weights reflect a blend of market-cap scale and thematic purity. Infineon Technologies (IFX.DE) and STMicroelectronics (STM) anchor the index at roughly 14.7% and 13.8% respectively — both vertically integrated *SiC MOSFET* manufacturers with multi-year EV supply agreements. STMicro supplies Renault’s (RNO.PA) Ampere division with SiC powerbox modules for 800V platforms; onsemi (ON), also at 13.8%, claims design wins in 60% of Chinese EV models through its EliteSiC platform and has expanded into 900V architectures in a collaboration with Geely Automobile (0175.HK). Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR) and Analog Devices (ADI) enter the basket primarily through data-centre power management; Texas Instruments (TXN) demonstrated a full 800V-to-processor conversion chain at NVIDIA GTC in March 2026. At the other end of the spectrum, Navitas and Wolfspeed each hold 5.18% — a cap that likely reflects liquidity constraints on small-cap positions. The remaining four — Flex Ltd (FLEX), Power Integrations (POWI), Vertiv Holdings (VRT), and Eaton Corp (ETN) — represent the systems-integration and power-distribution layer between chip and rack.

Wolfspeed’s presence is the most pointed element. The company controls the most strategically critical bottleneck in the 800V supply chain: *SiC substrates*. Every SiC chip maker in the basket depends on high-quality SiC wafers, and Wolfspeed held roughly 34% of the global substrate market in 2024 while operating the only 200mm SiC device fab at volume scale. That structural position survived the balance-sheet collapse. The Chapter 11 was prepackaged and resolved in 91 days, eliminating roughly 70% of the company’s $4.6bn in debt; an unexpected $698m IRS settlement in December 2025 provided additional cash relief. Renesas Electronics (6723.T) emerged with 38.7% of the reorganised equity; existing shareholders were left with roughly 3–5%. That Morgan Stanley’s index administrators kept Wolfspeed in the basket — rather than substituting a cleaner-balance-sheet peer — signals that 800V substrate supply is regarded as too structurally critical to remove. The reorganised WOLF shares, trading near $38 as of May 2026, are the instrument the basket holds: a post-emergence equity, not the pre-petition paper.

Two risks cut across the basket. Chinese producers have moved aggressively into SiC: SICC (688234.SS) and TanKeBlue collectively hold more than 34% of global substrate capacity, up from near-zero before 2020, and BYD Co (1211.HK) supplies SiC devices internally through a captive semiconductor subsidiary, bypassing index constituents for the world’s largest EV maker. The second risk is cyclical: following the 2019–2024 SiC investment supercycle, substrate and *epitaxy* utilisation rates have fallen to roughly 50%, with the trough expected to persist until 2027–2028 when 8-inch wafer platforms reach volume production. The data-centre opportunity softens both concerns — AI infrastructure demand is largely insulated from Chinese EV dynamics — but any structured product linked to MSXX800V ultimately bets that hyperscaler 800V conversion timelines align with the SiC industry’s own recovery.

concepts.definition: A compound semiconductor with a wider energy bandgap than silicon, allowing operation at higher voltages, temperatures, and switching frequencies. In power electronics, SiC MOSFETs handle the switching duties in EV traction inverters and power converters that silicon devices cannot sustain at 800V — an 800V battery bus requires 1,200V-rated switches to safely handle transient overvoltages during switching.

Another wide-bandgap semiconductor, typically grown on silicon wafers. GaN transistors switch faster than SiC at medium voltages (roughly 100–650V), making them well-suited for the DC-DC converter stages within 800V systems — stepping 800V bus voltage down to intermediate levels — rather than the main high-power traction inverter.

In a data-centre context, HVDC means distributing power at 800V DC directly from main switchgear to server racks, bypassing the multiple AC-to-DC conversion stages used in traditional 480V AC or 54V DC architectures. Each eliminated conversion stage recovers heat losses; at gigawatt scale the efficiency gain is material and the copper reduction is dramatic.

A metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor fabricated on silicon carbide. MOSFETs are the dominant switching device in modern power converters; the SiC variant can handle the 1,200V voltage ratings required when a battery bus or data-centre distribution bus operates at 800V. The key figure of merit is RDS(on) — on-state resistance — which determines heat dissipation during conduction.

The polished silicon carbide crystal wafer on which SiC power devices are grown via epitaxy. Producing large-diameter, low-defect-density SiC substrates is the most technically demanding step in the supply chain — defects propagate into the active device layers and reduce yield. This bottleneck gives substrate makers unusual pricing leverage over the downstream chip industry.

A debt security issued by a bank whose return is linked to the performance of a reference asset — here, a proprietary equity basket. Unlike a plain bond, the investor’s repayment may be contingent on the basket staying above certain price levels. Structured notes can be configured as autocallables, reverse convertibles, or principal-protected products, giving issuers flexibility in shaping risk-return profiles.

A type of structured note that is automatically redeemed early — at a preset premium — if the reference asset closes above a trigger level on predetermined observation dates. If it does not, the note continues; if the asset falls sharply and breaches a lower barrier, the investor absorbs the equity-like downside. Autocallables are among the most common structured products sold to private-wealth clients.

The process of growing a thin, single-crystal semiconductor layer on top of a substrate wafer. For SiC devices, the epitaxial layer defines the electrical characteristics of the finished transistor. Epitaxy is a distinct manufacturing step from substrate production with its own yield constraints; industry analysts track substrate and epitaxy utilisation rates separately when assessing supply-chain health.

ticker_wolf.name: Wolfspeed, Inc.
ticker_wolf.blurb: Wolfspeed designs and manufactures silicon carbide (SiC) power devices and substrates, positioning itself as the only vertically integrated producer at 200mm SiC wafer scale. Carved out of Cree in 2021, the company bet heavily on the EV and industrial power transition, sinking billions into the John Palmour Manufacturing Center in North Carolina and the Mohawk Valley Fab in New York. The ambition was sound; the balance sheet was not. After accumulating roughly $4.6 billion in debt and missing the expected CHIPS Act funding of $750 million, Wolfspeed filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on June 30, 2025. It emerged ninety-one days later in a prepackaged restructuring that eliminated ~70% of its debt, extended maturities to 2030, and cut annual cash interest expense by roughly 60%. Existing shareholders received only 3–5% of the reorganised equity; the bulk went to convertible noteholders (56.3%) and strategic investor Renesas (38.7%), who received new common stock plus warrants.
ticker_wolf.recent: Post-emergence, the reorganised Wolfspeed trades on NYSE under WOLF. The company's enterprise value at emergence was estimated at $2.35–2.85 billion (midpoint $2.6B), implying equity of $850M–$1.35B. As of May 2026 shares trade near $38. A December 2025 IRS settlement worth roughly $698 million provided unexpected cash relief. Chinese SiC substrate producers SICC (688234.SS) and TanKeBlue have gained market share during Wolfspeed's restructuring, while Infineon, STMicroelectronics, onsemi, and Rohm continue to invest in competing SiC capacity.

ticker_nvts.name: Navitas Semiconductor Corporation
ticker_nvts.blurb: Navitas Semiconductor Corporation designs, develops, and markets next-generation power semiconductors, specializing in gallium nitride (GaN) power integrated circuits and silicon carbide (SiC) power devices alongside silicon system controllers and digital isolators. Founded in 2014 and headquartered in Torrance, California, the company targets high-growth end markets including automotive, data centers, mobile, and consumer electronics. With roughly 190 employees, Navitas is a pure-play GaN/SiC challenger competing against legacy silicon power device incumbents such as Infineon, ON Semiconductor, and STMicroelectronics. The company remains pre-profitability, posting a net loss of ~$134M on trailing-twelve-month revenue of ~$40.5M.
ticker_nvts.recent: NVTS shares surged roughly 10% on May 13, 2026 — the day before this entry was written — closing at $21.17, near its 52-week high of $23.82 and well above its 52-week low of $1.88, implying a dramatic multi-month recovery. The company reported earnings on May 5, 2026; trailing revenue is down approximately 45% year-over-year, reflecting ongoing demand weakness in consumer and mobile end markets. Despite the price run-up, the consensus analyst price target of ~$12.88 sits roughly 39% below the current market price, suggesting Wall Street remains cautious relative to the market's recent enthusiasm.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.

ticker_stm.name: STMicroelectronics N.V.
ticker_stm.blurb: STMicroelectronics is a global semiconductor group covering microcontrollers, sensors (MEMS), and — most relevant to the AI power-plumbing thesis — a broad power-semiconductor portfolio spanning SiC MOSFETs (STPOWER Gen 4), GaN devices, silicon IGBTs, and power-management ICs. ST is one of only a handful of vendors with an end-to-end 800 VDC power-conversion solution for AI data centres, offering complete reference designs from 800V bus-to-50V, 12V, and 6V conversion using its own SiC and GaN silicon. The company serves automotive, industrial, and, increasingly, hyperscale data-centre customers.
ticker_stm.recent: ST reported Q1 2026 revenue of $3.10 billion, up 23% year-over-year and above consensus of $3.04 billion, with Q2 2026 guidance of ~$3.45 billion. In March 2026 the company announced expanded 800 VDC power-conversion products (12V and 6V architectures) developed to the NVIDIA 800 VDC reference design and showcased at NVIDIA GTC 2026. In February 2026 ST disclosed a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar engagement with Amazon Web Services to supply semiconductors for AWS compute and AI data-centre infrastructure. Management projects data-centre revenue exceeding $500 million in 2026 and surpassing $1 billion in 2027.

ticker_on.name: onsemi (ON Semiconductor Corporation)
ticker_on.blurb: onsemi designs and manufactures intelligent power and sensing semiconductors, with a particular focus on silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs and modules under the EliteSiC brand, IGBT power modules, intelligent power modules (IPMs), and gate drivers. The company is a dominant SiC supplier to EV traction inverters and has been rapidly expanding into AI data-centre power delivery, supplying high-efficiency SiC and MOSFET solutions for GPU server power stages. Onsemi claims to be the first vendor to scale vertical GaN production, with 700V and 1,200V devices addressing AI server PSU and rack-level power conversion.
ticker_on.recent: Onsemi reported Q1 2026 revenue of $1.513 billion, above the guidance midpoint, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.64 versus the $0.61 consensus. Q2 2026 revenue guidance was set at $1.535–$1.635 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $0.65–$0.77. Management reiterated an expectation that AI data-centre revenue will double year-over-year across all of 2026, supported by broader chip-vendor adoption of EliteSiC and new 900V SiC design wins with EV/ESS customers including Geely, NIO, and Sineng Electric.

ticker_mpwr.name: Monolithic Power Systems, Inc.
ticker_mpwr.blurb: A fab-light analog company that designs high-density power-management integrated circuits — the chips that step a server's intermediate-bus voltage down to the sub-1-volt rail an AI accelerator actually consumes. MPWR moved from a broad-based analog supplier into the dominant provider of GPU-adjacent power modules during the H100 generation, displacing the incumbent Vicor at Nvidia. Its modules are characterised by very high current density and tight integration, which matter enormously as AI racks push past 100 kilowatts.
ticker_mpwr.recent: In early 2026, management raised the floor on its enterprise-data growth target to 50-percent-plus from a prior 30-to-40 percent range, citing acceleration in Nvidia Blackwell shipments. Analyst notes suggest MPWR may take roughly 70 percent of power-management sockets on the forthcoming Vera Rubin GPU platform (VR200 NVL144 and R200 HGX), potentially adding more than $100 million to 2026 estimates. The stock has gained roughly 90 percent over the trailing twelve months and trades near all-time highs, leaving the AI exposure largely in the price.

ticker_adi.name: Analog Devices, Inc.
ticker_adi.blurb: Analog Devices is one of the two largest analog semiconductor companies in the world (alongside Texas Instruments), with deep expertise in signal-chain ICs, data converters, and — critical for AI servers — power-management products including hot-swap controllers, multiphase voltage regulators, power-system management ICs (PSMICs), and DC-DC power stages. ADI's LTC4284/4286/4287 hot-swap family protects 48V AI rack infrastructure, while its MAX20790 and related multiphase controllers regulate power to GPUs and accelerators at the point-of-load. The company is also a leading supplier of 800 VDC first-stage conversion solutions designed to NVIDIA's high-voltage DC reference architecture for AI factories.
ticker_adi.recent: ADI reported Q1 FY2026 (quarter ending January 2026) EPS of $2.46 versus the $2.31 consensus, with revenue of $3.16 billion supported by a 50% year-over-year increase in data-centre revenue. AI and data-centre exposure now accounts for roughly one-fifth of total revenues. Q2 FY2026 guidance was set at $3.5 billion (±$100 million), with non-GAAP EPS of $2.88 (±$0.15) and adjusted operating margin of ~47.5%. In August 2025 ADI announced its first 800 VDC hot-swap and first-stage power solutions targeting NVIDIA intelligent platform management, with >98% conversion efficiency. The company has seen accelerating adoption of 48V/54V intermediate-bus converters and smart power stages for vertical power delivery in AI racks.

ticker_txn.name: Texas Instruments Incorporated
ticker_txn.blurb: The largest pure-play analog-semiconductor maker in the world by revenue, with roughly twenty percent share of the analog market. Texas Instruments designs and manufactures power-management chips, signal-chain devices and embedded processors used in industrial machinery, automobiles and, increasingly, AI servers. Its strategy is unusual in the industry: it owns and operates several 300-millimetre wafer fabs in the United States, giving it a long-term cost advantage against fab-light competitors, but also requiring a multi-year capital-spending programme that compressed free cash flow through 2023-2024.
ticker_txn.recent: Q1 2026 revenue came in at $4.83 billion, ahead of the $4.53 billion consensus, with analog-segment revenue up 22 percent year on year and data-centre revenue up roughly 90 percent. Capital expenditure dropped 40 percent year on year to $676 million as the 300mm fab build-out tapers, and free cash flow rose to $1.40 billion. The company has also announced selective price increases of 15 to 85 percent on certain analog products effective April 2026, in line with similar moves by Analog Devices, Infineon and Murata. The stock is up roughly 50 percent year-to-date through April 2026.

ticker_flex.name: Flex Ltd.
ticker_flex.blurb: Flex Ltd. is a global advanced manufacturing and supply chain solutions company headquartered in Austin, Texas. The company designs, engineers, and manufactures complex products for premier brands across diversified end markets including automotive, healthcare, industrial, and consumer electronics. Flex operates at global scale, providing end-to-end services from product design through distribution. Over the past several years the company has repositioned itself as a technology-focused industrial manufacturer, divesting non-core assets and concentrating on higher-margin, complex manufacturing programs.
ticker_flex.recent: On May 5, 2026, Flex announced that its Board of Directors unanimously approved a plan to spin off its Cloud and Power Infrastructure segment into a new independent publicly traded company ('SpinCo'), intended to be tax-free to shareholders and targeted to close in Q1 calendar 2027. SpinCo will focus on power and thermal management technologies and integrated infrastructure systems for AI data centers and mission-critical applications, while Flex will continue as a focused advanced manufacturing company.
